description: Building a web app for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It lets mission planners, students and the public compare Moon landing sites and dates. It shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon, to judge solar power and direct-to-Earth communication windows. The plan includes a site and date picker, a timeline of sunlight and Earth visibility across a lunar day, and a side-by-side comparison view.
summary: Shackleton Ridge is a web app that compares Moon landing sites and dates by what a lander would actually see. For any site near the lunar south pole, it draws the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon using NASA LRO elevation data. It then measures how much sunlight and direct-to-Earth contact a lander gets over a mission window, and compares up to four site and date scenarios side by side. It covers 28 curated sites plus any custom coordinates. For example, at a site on the Mons Mouton Plateau, slipping the launch by three days doubles the sunlight of a 6.5 day stay. Results are checked against JPL Horizons and published studies. Built with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) under team direction.
details:
Shackleton Ridge helps mission planners, students and the public judge landing sites by the two things a lander depends on: sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth for communication.

What it does: pick a site and a date range. The app draws the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, then plots sunlight and Earth visibility across the mission window. Views include Explore, Compare (up to four scenarios), Launch slip, Map, Power budget, Mast height, and Better spot nearby. There are 28 curated sites plus custom coordinates.

How it works: Sun and Earth positions come from NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440 and the lunar orientation kernels), converted into the Moon-fixed frame. Horizon masks come from LRO LOLA south pole elevation models. Elevation and azimuth are computed in the browser.

Validation: Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons to about 0.0002 degrees. Illumination results were compared with Gläser et al. 2018 and the PGDA 18.6 year illumination maps.

Limits: terrain is modeled only from 60 S to the pole. Elevation error can shift grazing sunrise and sunset by hours. The app does not model lander shadow or relay satellites.

Tools: React, Vite, TypeScript, Leaflet, and Python (SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio) for the data pipeline. Code is MIT licensed.

Source code: https://github.com/H4ch1Net/lunar-landing-site-navigator

AI use: part of the code and text were written with help from Claude (Anthropic) under team direction, then reviewed, debugged, tested and fixed. All numbers in the app come from NASA data and the listed validation, not from an AI model. The demo video is a screen recording with a "Made with AI assistance" mark. No AI image, video or voice generator was used.
